strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing genuine limitation of QMIA (fails to capture epistemic uncertainty); clear problem formulation with effective toy example (Figure 1)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5 datasets, multiple baselines, thorough ablations (sample size, Hessian factorization, hyperparameters) and robustness tests (model mismatch, OOD)
Solid theoretical justification: Propositions 4.1-4.2 with sound proofs explain why conditional attacks outperform marginal attacks; uncertainty decomposition (Eq. 10) connects to attack power
Practical significance: 8× computational reduction vs. LiRA while maintaining competitive or superior performance
Good experimental setup following prior work conventions, enabling fair comparison; honest limitations section
weaknesses: Critical discrepancy between claims and results: Abstract claims 37.5% TPR at 1% FPR on CIFAR-10 with 64% improvement, but Table 1 shows only 8.87% on CIFAR-10 and 35.75% on CIFAR-100; numbers do not reconcile

Limited technical novelty: Laplace approximation is well-established; straightforward application to MIA lacks fundamentally new insights; Propositions 4.1-4.2 are mostly standard inequality applications

Significant unjustified simplifications: (1) Last-layer Laplace is drastic approximation—no analysis of information loss from earlier layers; (2) Gaussian assumption on hinge scores not empirically validated; (3) Reference distribution matching non-member distribution assumed but not verified

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-run reporting despite small effect sizes (0.1-2% TPR); cannot assess statistical significance of reported improvements

Incomplete experimental analysis: No comparison to other single-model Bayesian methods (SWAG, VI, ensembles); unexplained phenomenon (ResNet-34 target performs best with ResNet-18 reference); computational breakdown not detailed
No code release or reproducibility statement; random seed management not discussed; limited ablation on reference model size and quality sensitivity

strengths: Clear motivation identifying real limitation of prior work (quantile regression missing epistemic uncertainty) with good illustrative example (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experiments across 5 datasets with multiple baselines and detailed implementation documentation in appendices
Significant computational efficiency gains: achieving competitive TPR at low FPR with 8x lower training cost than LiRA
Theoretical framework (Propositions 4.1-4.2) formalizing when/why conditional attacks outperform marginal attacks
Extensive implementation details for Laplace approximation including KFAC, last-layer variants, and hyperparameter tuning
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward application of well-established Laplace approximation techniques (Daxberger et al. 2021) to MIAs with no novel algorithmic or methodological contributions

Proposition 4.2 proof has significant gaps: Jensen's inequality validity only claimed 'under sufficiently small α' (never defined or validated), and subsequent algebraic manipulations are not clearly justified

Laplace approximation quality not validated: never verified that posterior approximation holds in practice for deep networks, that MAP is good optimum, or that local linearization (Eq. 14) is valid for ReLU networks

Unfair experimental comparisons: BMIA uses 1 reference model while baselines use 2-8, preventing fair computational budget comparison; no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing across multiple runs
Gaussian assumption for hinge scores (required for t-test validity) never empirically validated despite being critical; no Q-Q plots or normality diagnostics provided

Central motivation is undermined by empirical results: QMIA performs comparably to BMIA in many settings (Purchase-100: 0.11% vs 0.71% at 0.1% FPR), suggesting the epistemic uncertainty issue may not materialize in practice
Significant vulnerability to architectural mismatch (Figure 4) where performance degrades to ~10^-4 at 0.1% FPR with different architectures, but this practical limitation is minimally discussed

Incomplete ablation studies: no systematic comparison of full-layer vs last-layer Laplace quality, missing sensitivity analysis for sample size N, no comparison with other BNN methods (VI, MCMC, ensembles)
Reproducibility concerns: code not mentioned as available, reference dataset size unclear, number of experimental runs/trials not specified, dependency versions not documented
OOD robustness insufficient (Table 2): performance drops from 2.28% to 1.62% TPR with OOD non-members but issue is barely discussed; no analysis of distribution shift robustness

strengths: Clear motivation: Effectively identifies and illustrates the limitation of QMIA in capturing epistemic uncertainty in low-density regions through intuitive toy example (Figure 1)
Strong practical efficiency gains: Achieves state-of-the-art results with 1/8 training cost compared to LiRA (n=8), particularly impressive at low FPR (0.1-1%) where privacy matters most

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Five datasets, six baselines, thorough ablations (sample size, Hessian approximations, hyperparameter tuning), robustness checks (mismatched architectures, OOD samples)
Sound methodology: Well-designed Bayesian framework with formal theoretical justification (Propositions 4.1-4.2) connecting uncertainty quantification to attack power
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across datasets (e.g., CIFAR-100: 13.11% vs 6.23% TPR@0.1% FPR for LiRA n=8) with detailed performance reporting
Good reproducibility: Clear implementation details, algorithm pseudocode, extensive appendices, promised code availability via laplace library
Theoretical grounding: Clear decomposition of epistemic vs aleatoric uncertainty with proper connection to conditional attack effectiveness
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Laplace approximation for BNNs is well-established; applying to MIAs is relatively straightforward application of existing technique without significant methodological innovation

Shallow theoretical contributions: Propositions 4.1-4.2 are direct applications of standard probability theory and Jensen's inequality; proofs lack depth and don't explain why BNNs are fundamentally better beyond uncertainty quantification
Experimental design concerns: Unclear whether reference models across all baselines use identical data splits; potential unfairness in comparison if reference datasets differ in size or composition

Unvalidated core assumptions: Heavy reliance on Gaussian assumptions for score distributions not empirically validated across datasets; Laplace approximation's local nature and sensitivity to poor local minima not analyzed
Algorithm design choices under-justified: One-sample t-test in Algorithm 1 not well-motivated; no exploration of alternative statistical tests or score difference formulations (d_i = s_0 - s_i)
Inconsistent results: On some datasets (e.g., Purchase-100 at 0.1% FPR), improvements over baselines are marginal, undermining strong claims of superiority
Limited robustness analysis: OOD evaluation restricted to CINIC-10; no evaluation on models with adversarial training, mixup, or other regularization schemes
Missing technical comparisons: No comparison with alternative uncertainty quantification methods (temperature scaling, conformal prediction, ensemble-based approaches) or other BNN approximations

strengths: Novel application of Laplace approximation to membership inference attacks, enabling efficient conditional attacks with a single reference model while maintaining competitive effectiveness

Comprehensive theoretical analysis, including previously missing formal justification for why conditional attacks outperform marginal attacks (Proposition B.2) and insightful variance decomposition into intra-model and inter-model components

Extensive experimental evaluation across 10 datasets spanning three modalities with multiple strong baselines, thorough ablation studies, and robustness analysis (architecture mismatch, OOD samples, distribution shift)
Significant practical improvements: achieves 35.75% TPR at 1% FPR on CIFAR-100 with 1/8 the computational cost of LiRA (n=8), making privacy auditing more accessible
Well-executed presentation with clear algorithms, proper ablations, honest reporting of both effectiveness and efficiency, and comprehensive appendices with proofs and implementation details
weaknesses: Layered approximations (Laplace → last-layer restriction → Hessian factorization) whose combined effect on posterior quality lacks theoretical analysis; unclear how much information is lost restricting probabilistic inference to last-layer parameters
Limited novelty in core methodology—the conditional MIA framework is inherited from LiRA/Attack-R; the contribution is primarily in efficient estimation rather than new attack concepts

Theoretical-empirical gap: Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 don't fully explain why Bayesian posterior sampling is fundamentally superior to simpler parametric distribution fitting to reference scores; connection between variance reduction and empirical TPR improvement is intuitive but not rigorous

Critical gap in evaluation: no robustness testing against privacy-preserving training methods (differential privacy, regularization); unclear if BMIA remains effective against DP-SGD or other practical defenses

Heavy reliance on Gaussian assumption for t-test validity; while Figure 5 provides empirical support, limited exploration of failure modes or comprehensive handling beyond mentioning conformal p-values in appendix
Experiments on relatively modest-scale models (ResNet-50, DenseNet-121); statistical significance testing absent in main results with most comparisons lacking error bars or confidence intervals
Minimal discussion of ethical implications and practical defenses; impact statement dismisses societal concerns; no guidance for practitioners on mitigating these attacks

Incomplete analysis of design choices: limited exploration of hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., prior variance γ), alternative score functions, or explanation of robustness in architecture mismatch scenarios

strengths: Practical efficiency gains: Achieves competitive attack performance with 1/8th computational cost compared to multi-reference baselines, addressing real deployment concerns
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10 datasets in 3 modalities with thorough ablations, robustness checks (OOD, architecture mismatch, distribution shift)
Solid theoretical grounding: Variance decomposition (Proposition 3.1) provides good intuition; Appendix B fills gap by formally analyzing why conditional attacks outperform marginal attacks
Principled statistical framework: Uses proper hypothesis testing with Student's t-statistics and Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom rather than ad-hoc thresholds
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written paper with extensive appendices and promised code release; implementation details well-documented
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is straightforward application of existing techniques (Laplace approximation + hypothesis testing). Theoretical results (variance decomposition, connection to statistical power) are standard and incremental

Unjustified critical assumption: Equation (10) assumes Var(s₀) = Var(sᵢ) with minimal justification. Why should target and reference model scores have equal variance? This assumption is fundamental to the t-test but inadequately discussed

Last-layer Laplace approximation is a significant limitation: Only quantifies uncertainty in final layer, ignoring substantial parameter uncertainty in feature extractors of deep networks. No analysis of approximation quality or empirical comparison with full Laplace

Misleading baseline comparisons: Main Table 1 compares single-reference BMIA against multi-reference methods (n=8), obscuring whether BMIA truly outperforms single-reference baseline RMIA (buried in Table 2). Efficiency gains come from fewer models, not better attack algorithm

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Theorem 3.2 (more samples → lower variance → higher power) is obvious from the variance formula. No convergence rates, finite-sample bounds, or analysis of robustness when Gaussian assumption violated

Gaussian assumption validation insufficient: Empirical diagnostics (Figure 5) only on CIFAR datasets. No analysis of heavy-tailed score distributions. Fallback to conformal p-values mentioned but not implemented

Missing calibration validation: No empirical demonstration that nominal false positive rates (α) are actually achieved. No coverage analysis under model misspecification. Only Table 9 reports variance (CIFAR-10 only)

QMIA critique lacks rigor: Appendix D argues QMIA misses epistemic uncertainty using toy example (Figure 4), but QMIA performs competitively on many real datasets in Table 1, contradicting the dismissal

strengths: Strong practical contribution: Achieves 54% improvement over LiRA on CIFAR-100 with 8× lower computational cost, addressing real bottleneck in privacy auditing

Solid theoretical analysis: Elegant variance decomposition (Proposition 3.1), formal proof that more samples improve attack power (Theorem 3.2), and missing theoretical justification for conditional vs. marginal attacks (Appendix B)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests across 10 datasets spanning three modalities, includes ablation studies, robustness analysis (architecture mismatch, OOD samples, dataset shift), and computational cost comparisons
Well-executed presentation: Clear motivation, rigorous mathematical exposition, complete algorithms, comprehensive appendices, and effective visual demonstrations (especially Figure 3)
Flexible framework: Naturally extends to multi-reference setting (MR-BMIA) when additional computational budget is available, showing generalizability
weaknesses: Incremental core technical novelty: Primarily applies existing Laplace approximation to MIA rather than developing new methodology; the contribution is recognizing this fit rather than technical innovation

Gaussian distribution assumption for validity: Method assumes hinge scores are approximately Gaussian for Student's t-test validity; while empirically supported (Figure 5), assumption validity across diverse settings not thoroughly validated, and suggested non-Gaussian calibration (conformal p-values) is mentioned but not empirically evaluated

Restrictive reference dataset requirements: Assumes access to non-member data from similar distribution; Section 4.4 shows notable performance degradation with distribution mismatch (CINIC-10 vs CIFAR-10); no guidance on acceptable divergence limits

Last-layer Laplace approximation limitations: Only treats final layer weights probabilistically; may limit uncertainty quantification on very deep models; no evaluation on billion-parameter networks where this tradeoff could matter more
Incomplete reproducibility: Code availability statement (page 1) has URL cut off; verification of actual code release needed

Limited failure mode analysis: Minimal discussion of underperformance cases, poorly-calibrated models, or sensitivity to Hessian approximation quality; text dataset results are more modest (1.75-7.90% at 0.1% FPR) without deep investigation
Comparison fairness concerns: n=1 BMIA compared against n=2,4,8 baselines makes direct comparison difficult; QMIA has different computational profiles that complicate fair assessment
Missing practical context: No discussion of model hardening strategies or defenses; no evaluation on how attack performs against models with differential privacy or strong regularization
